newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish banker sees economy stable in 1st half '97.
newsitem.headline: Turkish banker sees economy stable in 1st half '97.

text.p: The Turkish economy is expected to follow a stable course in the first half of 1997 and banks are unlikely to seek radical changes in their government bond-dominated portfolios, a senior Turkish banker said.

"It is seen that there will be relative stability in the next two quarters. But this period is still less than the maturity of state papers traded on the market," Mustafa Gurtin, head of Garanti Investment Bank, told Reuters in an interview.
Unlike some bankers who are concerned about possible political upheaval, Gurtin sees continued stability on the political side.
"The possibility of a market crisis triggered by political turmoil is very low," he said.

After months of political crisis and government deadlock, Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party formed a coalition with Tansu Ciller's centre-right True Path Party last June on the basis of a rotating premiership.
Some political analysts think Erbakan may dissolve the partnership before Ciller takes office in 1998.
"Welfare will not break up the coalition unless it prepares an alternative," Gurtin said.
Under Erbakan's administration the Treasury has extended its average borrowing maturity and lowered interest rates.
Maturities have risen to 13 months from six and yields declined to 112.4 percent from 144.9 percent in mid-November. Year-on-year consumer price inflation was 79.8 percent in 1996.
Gurtin said interest rates have bottomed out. "It is seen that interest rates will remain at present levels for about one month," he added.

Despite lower interest rates, Gurtin, a former central bank fund manager, said "Government borrowing papers are still an attractive investment instrument particularly for banks which have made really good profits in the past few years. The system does not plan to give up bonds."
The Treasury has been offering high real interest rates of up to 40 points to borrow from the markets since early 1994, when the country was hit by a financial crisis.
The government wants to narrow the gap between inflation and treasury borrowing rates. But bankers say any substantial decline is unlikely unless chronic inflation is pulled down.

Turkey has also been one of the markets favoured by foreign investors, who benefit from the margin between high domestic interest rates and relatively lower lira depreciation, about 46 percent against the dollar in 1996.
Gurtin said the West was still in a wait-and-see mood as far as the Islamist-led government was concerned. "They are very cool and tolerant."

He said any deal between Turkey and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would increase Turkey's credibility in international markets. "But it will not be a catastrophe for Turkey if the IMF does not give the green light," he added.
Turkey and the IMF will resume talks in late January or early February, officials say.
